# Locating and Accessing the Idle Air Control Valve on a Renault Clio Mk2

Stalling issues while decelerating to a stop are one of the most common symptoms of a failing or clogged Idle Air Control (IAC) valve on 1998–2000 model year Renault Clio Mk2s equipped with the 1.2L engine. The root cause is typically carbon buildup in the throttle body, which restricts the airflow path the ECU uses to maintain baseline RPM when the throttle plate closes. While online forums often point toward replacement as a quick fix, verifying the location and attempting a cleaning first can save significant money.

The IAC valve on this specific platform is not a standalone component mounted directly onto the intake manifold in a way that requires removing the entire air intake assembly. Instead, it is integrated into the throttle body itself. On the 1.2L engine found in these vehicles, the unit is located at the front of the engine bay, attached to the black plastic housing of the throttle body. You will identify it by a small cylindrical motor actuator protruding from the side or top of the throttle body assembly, usually secured with two bolts or clips depending on the specific sub-variant of the Mk2.

Accessing the valve does not require disassembling the air filter box or removing the upper radiator support, provided your engine bay layout matches standard configurations. However, there is a critical mechanical consideration before you attempt to swap the unit: clearance for the intake manifold bolts. On some later revisions of the 1.2L engine, the throttle body angle creates interference with the rear mounting points of the intake manifold if the valve housing is slightly misaligned or if new gaskets add thickness. Before removing any fasteners, inspect the gap between the throttle body flange and the intake manifold studs to ensure there isn't a binding issue that would prevent proper torque application later.

If you decide to remove the IAC motor for cleaning or replacement, disconnect the electrical connector first—these are typically simple push-type connectors but can be stiff. Once unbolted, gently pull the valve out of its bore in the throttle body. Do not force it; if it resists, check that you haven't stripped the retaining clip. The internal pintle mechanism is prone to sticking due to oil vapors from the PCV system or general road dust entering via the breather.

Cleaning should be done with a dedicated carburetor cleaner spray and a soft brush. Avoid using brake cleaner or solvents containing chlorinated hydrocarbons, as these can degrade the rubber seals inside the throttle body housing once reinstalled. After cleaning, operate the valve manually (if possible) to ensure the motor armature moves freely through its full range of motion without binding against the carbon deposit.

It is worth noting that while many sources suggest replacing the unit immediately upon cleaning failure, simply swapping a new IAC without addressing underlying vacuum leaks or checking the throttle position sensor (TPS) calibration will likely result in immediate recurrence of stalling. The ECU learns idle positions based on feedback from the TPS; if the sensor drifts, the valve works harder to compensate, leading to premature wear. Ensure the throttle body is free of debris before reassembly and verify that the new or cleaned unit seats flush against the housing to maintain a proper seal around the intake manifold gasket.

For those looking for further technical documentation on Renault engine management systems, you might find additional context at https://laravelcompany.com regarding modern diagnostic approaches, though the mechanical principles for the Mk2 remain largely analog and robust compared to later D4 or dCi variants.
